sources.text: The 2026 Game Award nominations have finally been revealed. This is arguably one of the biggest years in gaming, as it has featured some of the hottest, most anticipated games out there. We got the long-awaited return of Leon Kennedy in Resident Evil Requiem, the release of 007 First Light, which fans had been waiting for since 2020, and, of course, the launch of GTA 6. With the year coming to an end, The Game Awards has revealed the nominees for 2026 ahead of the ceremony on December 10. As you might have predicted, GTA 6 swept with eight nominations, including the coveted Game of the Year. Yes, we really got GTA 6 nominated for Game of the Year before GTA 6. There's it's competing with 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake for the main award. The Game Awards 2026 nominations also confirms, finally, the actor who plays Lucia in GTA 6 . Manni L. Perez, who many fans had suspected played Lucia in Rockstar's game, is nominated in the Best Performance category. The actor who plays fellow GTA 6 protagonist Jason doesn't make the cut. Nintendo is The Game Awards’ most nominated publisher in 2026 with 12 nominations across its combined portfolio, followed by Capcom with 11 nominations, and Annapurna Interactive and PlayStation with nine nominations each. The Best Adaptation award includes noms for Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2, Fallout Season 2, Mortal Kombat II, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, and Resident Evil. Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

sources.title: 8 Biggest Snubs in the 2026 Game Awards Nominations
sources.text: The Game Awards has announced its official list of nominees for this year’s prizes. Among the nominees are plenty of obvious contenders, such as Grand Theft Auto 6 , Resident Evil Requiem , and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time . There was stiff competition across several categories, meaning that some worthy games — and Polygon favorites — didn’t make the shortlist for certain prizes. These are the biggest TGA nomination snubs of 2026. As one eagle-eyed Resetera user pointed out, Sony just broke a streak that dates all the way back to 2015. This marks the first time in 11 years that a first-party PlayStation release hasn't received a Game of the Year nomination. During that 11-year streak, Sony took home three GOTY trophies: God of War (2018), The Last of Us Part 2 (2020), and Astro Bot (2024). This year's big first-party game from PlayStation was Marvel's Wolverine , which is currently sitting at a 75 on Metacritic and incited a whole lot of debate about difficulty and UI design. The game was nominated in two categories: Best Performance for Liam McIntyre and Innovation in Accessibility. This outcome won't come as a surprise to Polygon's Oli Welsh, who predicted Marvel's Wolverine missing out on a GOTY nomination and snapping Sony's impressive streak all the way back in September. There were a ton of fantastic video game performances this year, and somebody’s favorite was bound to get left out. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave fan favorite Jimmie Yamaguchi gave an outstanding performance as the oddball scholar Fabio, and by every measure, it deserved a nomination. In less capable hands, Fabio’s starry-eyed devotion to Fortune’s Weave co-protagonist Dietrich could have been played for laughs, but Yamaguchi makes the budding romance between these men believable and heartfelt. Manni L. Perez was nominated for GTA 6, presumably for portraying Lucia Caminos. (Funnily enough, developer Rockstar Games has not yet officially confirmed Perez is actually playing Lucia, despite longstanding online rumors.) Apparently, the actor who played co-lead Jason Duval didn’t make enough of an impact with players to score a nomination. Blizzard’s World of Warcraft has had a massive year, with the launch of its reimagined Classic experience, World of Warcraft: Forever . The team also released major updates for the modern version of the beloved MMORPG, like March’s Midnight expansion. Those changes weren’t enough to move the needle with voters, and WoW was also left out of the Best Community Support category. The popular farming sim, which entered early access in 2024 before its full release this year, may have more than 26,000 “overwhelmingly positive” reviews on Steam, but that wasn’t enough for it to snag a nomination in any category. Best Debut Indie might have been Fields of Mistria ’s best shot at a prize, but it wouldn’t have been out of place in Best Sim/Strategy or the broader Best Indie category, either. Despite a wobbly third act, Fortune’s Weave is one of our favorite games of 2026, one of the best games available for the Nintendo Switch 2, and one of the best-reviewed games of the year . Surprisingly, developer Intelligent Systems’ epic strategy RPG only managed to pick up one nomination, for Best Role-Playing Game. It stands a decent chance of taking this one home: other nominees include Final Fantasy Resonance, Monster Hunter Stories 3, The Blood of Dawnwalker , and Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter . Pearl Abyss’s open-world adventure game was an early-year frontrunner for a GOTY nom, even after middling reviews and a rocky launch. While it wasn’t a critical darling, it did have a pretty massive online following that made the prospect of several nominations seem likely. Surprisingly, Crimson Desert will compete in just one category: Best Community Support. Bungie’s extraction shooter managed to snag a nomination for Best Multiplayer Game, which it frankly stands little chance of winning against a field that includes two indie chart-toppers and a well-regarded Call of Duty. However, the stylish game was overlooked in the Best Art Direction category, perhaps partly due to the shadow cast by a 2025 plagiarism scandal where Bungie admitted to using an artist’s designs without proper credit. (Bungie later credited her as a Visual Design Consultant.) Marathon ’s retro-future meets Y2K cyberpunk aesthetic truly stands out in a sea of Unreal Engine 5 homogeneity, and it’s a shame to see it overlooked here. Both the Best Indie and Best Debut Indie categories have some stiff competition this year. However, no independent game managed to get a nomination for Game of the Year in 2026. While there weren’t a ton of indie contenders for the top category this year, Polygon’s Oli Welsh had the co-op adventure Big Walk pegged as a dark horse , though developer House House’s recent AI controversy likely didn’t help matters. The lack of an indie GOTY nominee represents a pretty massive shift from the 2025 crop, which included a record-setting three games developed by independent studios: Hades 2, Hollow Knight: Silksong, and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 . Sandfall Interactive’s much-loved RPG managed to take home the top prize and a total of nine Game Awards, the most wins by a single game. 2024 also saw one indie crack the category, Balatro , though the top honors went to Astro Bot . The Game Awards 2026 will stream live on Disney+, YouTube, and Twitch, on Thursday, Dec. 10, starting at 7:30 p.m. EST / 4:30 p.m. PST.

sources.title: Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is GTA 5 without the finesse - so why is the 2004 classic such a strange delight to return to?
sources.text: There is a place in Whitewood Estates where a promising stretch of blacktop suddenly gives way to the desert. It feels like the road has been erased, a sentence left unfinished. It's quietly strange, a weird bit of urban wrongfooting. But I guess it makes some kind of sense. California, after all, is home to California City, a town that was planned and then never really built. It sits out there now, north of Los Angeles, streets laid out but slowly being eaten by the sand and dirt. Still, 14,000 people lived there as of 2018. Design limitation or something stranger, this digital dead end is a reminder that all of this land, so modern, so ancient - all of this is spook country. It's fitting I guess that GTA San Andreas is such a strange delight to return to. As I've waited, like everyone else, for GTA 6 , I've been back here in the GTA games of the past, via the slightly dodgy remasters from a few years ago. And what's come through for me, spending a few idle mornings messing around in San Andreas, a game I thought I knew pretty well, is how beautifully odd everything is now. The best part of 20 years have given a game that once strained against its host technology a genuine aesthetic. Surprisingly sparse in detailing, as angular and sheer as dream architecture, in love with expanses, San Andreas is perfectly placed, it seems to me, to capture just how weird California can be. California and Nevada. This is the part I always forget. I mainly think of San Andreas these days through the lens of GTA 5 , which gives you LA and its surroundings but lets the single city serve as the star. It has a bigger footprint than the earlier game, sure, but it uses that space to go deep on the detailing and the sense of a singular, fiercely specific place. San Andreas meanwhile offers three cities - and one of them isn't actually in California. Alongside spins on LA and San Francisco, you get a version of Las Vegas. It's quite neat really: the three points of some arcane spiritual triangle. The kind of thing Marvel Whiteside Parsons, aerospace engineer and Actual Wizard, might have scratched in the dust of his backyard to help him control the weather. He lived - and died - in Pasadena, so all this would have been familiar anyway. There is a classic moment in every GTA. A moment where the map opens up in the early games, or when you explore enough in the later games, and simply get to understand the audacity of what is being attempted here. In San Andreas, and this feels apt, the best way to have this moment is to break the rules, sneaking into the open map before the game is fully ready for you. An early mission allows you to step away from the critical path, as it were, and peg it to the airport in Los Santos, where a plane is waiting to be pinched. Taxi, feel the thrust, and you're off. LA beneath you - sorry, Los Santos - and on the horizon a dinkytown version of the Golden Gate Bridge and the MGM Grand. Dinkytown is the word. From the sky, the huge map of San Andreas, which still feels like an incredible piece of work - such ambition! - can look like toys laid out on a duvet in the remasters. Coming back from GTA 5, a masterpiece of texture, the cities of San Andreas in particular feel very weird - cramped and condensed and wonderfully stagey, arranged the way a kid might jury-rig them together from shoeboxes and stray cardboard. On your way out of Grove Street early on you pass the Los Santos equivalent of the Hollywood sign, looming so close the way it does in the movies but not in the actual city and you feel you could touch it. Downtown is reduced to a handful of the best buildings - it's always pleasing to see the one from the brilliant first act of Speed made the cut - but still manages to capture the important stuff too, which in this case is the way that modern LA looms somewhat cruelly over the old city, captured with a strange sepulchral dignity in the form of the City Hall, so easy to spot but now so small! Elsewhere, the ersatz Las Vega Strip looks like a drawing based on memory - a few of the classic shapes are there, but it's a sketch of a place. In this way, I guess, it captures a truth about Las Vegas. Also, perhaps, it's an admission that this is a town comfortably out of the reach of satire. As for San Francisco, it's a 60s cop movie delight to fishtail around. It nails the hills and what more do you need for a game with cars in it? Taken as a whole these cities feel mesmerising now. And it's the limitations that make them sing, I think: those sheer granite canyons of downtown LA with its towering blocks of architecture and surprisingly thin traffic, with only the very faintest of ambient soundtracks that ensures any gunfire will pop and clap and shake you out of your seat. (Remember, I am playing the remasters and sound effects may be missing.) This is the LA of Repo Man rather than Heat - an otherland where the buildings feel alien, even the air feels alien. At night, palm trees stand out against a sky that glows a deep, clean red. GTA 5 would finesse all of this, the skyboxes and whatnot, but perhaps in that finessing something is lost. (Both games, incidentally, have such a talent for capturing California's kitsch excess that they perhaps miss some of the sweeter truths, such as the astonishing diversity of cultures a city like Los Angeles finds homes for. But how could any game do that justice?) Dinkytowns aside, what San Andreas does better than GTA 5 is space - the peculiar flat spaces of Southern California in particular, a state in which you can never quite tell where the wilderness ends and the landscaping begins, and where the ancient rocks that announce the horizon can look new, like stage settings, while the freeways feel truly ancient, concrete lizards sleeping on the dirt, bleached by the easy sun. sources.text: The Game Awards says its judges "may be provided with advance or pre-release access to games for critical evaluation." The Game Awards has announced its nominations slate for 2026, revealing that Grand Theft Auto 6 is this year's most-nominated game. Rockstar's hotly anticipated crime epic has secured eight nominations including Game of the Year, for which it'll be competing with games including Resident Evil Requiem, Control Resonant, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Now you—and the countless other people preparing to argue about this online—may have noticed that GTA 6 has been nominated for a number of awards despite the fact that it hasn't been released yet . In a press release, The Game Awards notes that jurors were in some cases provided with early access to enable awards consideration. "The nominees for The Game Awards are selected by a global jury of over 160 media publications and creator outlets around the world, who may be provided with advance or pre-release access to games for critical evaluation," The Game Awards said. In a Variety interview last week, Game Awards host and co-creator Geoff Keighley refuted speculation that TGA 2026 eligibility deadlines had been sculpted to allow GTA 6 to have a shot for this year's nominations. "There was a thing a few weeks ago where everyone thought that we had changed our dates to accommodate GTA, and it's like, no, actually our dates have been very set every year. It's the same calendar that we have," Keighley said. "I don't know this, but I'm sure some of these companies consider that when they're looking at their release calendars." You can view and vote on the Game Awards nominees at the TGA website —but it's been crashing consistently since the nominees were announced, so we've collected all the nominees below. sources.text: Includes the return of Now & Later Packs, MLB The Show 26 community stats, and more. Before we dive into new information on MLB The Show 27, let’s take a look back. As we reflect on 2026, two things stand out above everything else: the incredible passion and support of the MLB The Show community, and our need to better communicate and react to community feedback going forward. Whether you’ve been playing for decades or joined us for the first time this year, you’ve helped make this another special chapter in our franchise’s history. While we’re proud of what our team accomplished this year, we recognize that the heart of MLB The Show has always been its community. Since launch, you’ve hit an astonishing: You’ve also drawn 123,300,616 walks and racked up a staggering 2,130,551,161 strikeouts. It seems we have some work to do on our collective plate discipline and pitch recognition! But it’s not all strikeouts. You’ve also recorded 18,666,758 Perfect-Perfect hits and scored an incredible 2,506,757,548 runs. And if those numbers weren’t impressive enough, the community collectively spent the equivalent of 31,541 years playing MLB The Show this year. This year was not without some issues and hopefully over the next few months we’ll show you how we’ve made improvements in a host of areas.Your stories, feedback, creativity, and passion remind us why we do what we do. sources.title: Sony Defeats $2.6 Billion Class-Action Lawsuit Over Claimed PlayStation Store Monopoly
sources.text: Since 2022 , Sony has been facing the British equivalent of a class action lawsuit that could have cost the company as much as $2.6 billion had it lost. It, however, did not. As reported byÂ The Game Business , the lawsuit brought by consumer advocate Alex Neill claimed that Sony was operating a “near monopoly” via the PlayStation Store, and sued the Japanese company on behalf of nine million UK PlayStation owners, but today the claims were rejected, and the case has been dismissed. The reported financial goal of the lawsuit has wildly swung about over the years, cited as $5.9 billion in 2022 , then $7.9 billion by 2023 , and then down to $2.6 billion in May of this year. Whatever the number, the case being made was that by not allowing third-party stores to sell digital PlayStation games, Sony effectively has a monopoly from which it extracts 30 percent of every sale. This, said Neill and the PlayStation You Owe Us campaign, was an “abuse” of Sony’s “dominant position,” forcing customers to pay “too much for digital games and in-game content purchased through the PlayStation Store.” A previous attempt to have the case thrown out was rejected in 2023, and then things looked far worse for Sony when it lost a very similar case in California in May of this year , to the tune of $7.8 billion. And there’s the rather pertinent point that Sony absolutely does dominate sales of digital games on PlayStation, and that’s only going to get a whole lot worse as the megacorp phases out physical media entirely. Yet, following May’s trial , London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal has rejected the argument and ruled that, as reported by TGB , “the claim failed to establish that PlayStation infringed competition law.” The argument against a monopoly was based on the wider competition of Xbox, Nintendo, and PC, alongside the (current) option to buy physical versions of games. Allowing third-party stores onto the PlayStation could, the court said, impact security, which interestingly was the failed argument Google made in its battle against Epic. The tribunal also said Neill had failed to prove that Sony’s profits were “excessive,” likely given that 30 percent cuts are pretty much an industry standard. However, Sony is still facing similar cases in Holland, Portugal, and Mexico, and it seems they could fall either way. Donât miss the latest reviews, news and tips. Sign up for our free newsletter. sources.title: PlayStation beats $2.6 billion lawsuit over its game prices
sources.text: PlayStation will not be compelled to allow third-party stores on its consoles A lawsuit brought against PlayStation over its storefront and game prices has been dismissed. The UK class action lawsuit was brought against PlayStation by Alex Neill,Â representing PlayStation users who complained that they were trapped and forced to use the PS Store. They argued that PlayStation’s 30% cut on all game sales led to games being sold for “excessive and unfair prices”. If PlayStation lost the lawsuit, the plaintiffs were seeking $2.6 billion in damages. As reported by The Game Business , Londonâs Competition Appeal Tribunal has rejected this argument entirely, dismissing the idea that PlayStation has a “near monopoly” on the market. However, part of its argument was that users could instead opt to buy games physically – something which will not remain the case for much longer. PlayStation says it will phase out physical game sales by January 2028 . With that said, PlayStation users might not have much more luck with this argument when physical games are phased out either. That is because the court was not convinced that PlayStation games were priced too highly on the PS Store, or that game prices would be brought down if PlayStation allowed third-party storefronts on its systems.Â PlayStation is facing similar lawsuits in other regions, so it remains to be seen if it can defeat all of them. If any of them were to side against the company, that could set a significant precedent in the gaming industry, opening all platform owners up to third-party storefronts. For the time being, though, the status quo has been maintained with this UK ruling. Right now, the big three console giants – PlayStation, Xbox , and Nintendo – all maintain their own storefronts on their platforms. The only exception to this is Valve , which allows users to buy games from other storefronts on the Steam Machine and Steam Deck. Xbox’s storefront is also available on PC , as is Xbox Game Pass.

sources.title: London court tosses $2.6 billion Sony lawsuit claiming it holds "near monopoly" on PlayStation Store
sources.text: The case was dismissed entirely and unanimously A $2.6 billion lawsuit alleging Sony holds a "near monopoly" through the PlayStation Store, and has used its position to charge more and extract "unfair" margins on sales, has been dismissed by the London Competition Appeal Tribunal. As The Game Business spotted, the class action-style case case was dismissed entirely via unanimous judgment . "The Class Representative has not satisfied us that Sony is dominant in any relevant market for the purposes of assessing any anti-competitive infringement by Sony," the concluding remarks read. The question was not whether Sony is dominant on the PlayStation Store. Of course Sony is king on its own platform. The court essentially examined whether that dominance creates or supports unfair, illegally monopolistic conditions. The court ruled that it does not, and for a variety of factors, including competition provided by physical game sales, as well as platforms like Xbox, Nintendo, and PC. Additionally, it found that letting third-party stores on the PlayStation platform would require "significant adaptation of the platform and its operations" at "significant cost and effort," likely leading to "reduced security in the platform architecture and with potentially reduced performance." The impending end of physical PlayStation games, with Sony looking to phase out discs for new games in January 2028, obviously looms over the discussion here. The court did acknowledge it, but only via post-trial submissions, as this lawsuit stretches back to 2022, far before Sony announced the end of discs. But I do think the court's comments are relevant and interesting in general. "If there is no substitution between physical and digital games, then a decision to cease physical sales would mean that those sales would be lost altogether," one snippet reads. "If there is a legitimate concern with this decision, it would be (contrary to the Class Representative's case) that it eliminates a competitive constraint on Sony from independent retailers and allows Sony to increase digital pricing once that constraint has gone." Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more That is, indeed, one concern with the end of discs: the physical market not only provides a potentially cheaper option and resale path, its existence also puts a leash on digital prices. Pertinently, Nintendo is selling some Switch 2 games $10 cheaper digitally as it reduces but does not remove its physical footprint in today's game-key card era. In the chunky court document, a whole SSNIP analysis – "A small, but significant, non-transitory increase in price of 5-10% – looks at whether "physical games are a substitute for digital games" and if such a digital price increase would drive PlayStation users to physical. Of course, we know where the court landed. Additionally, the judgment reads, "Even if Nintendo and gaming PCs are not within the relevant market, we think it very likely that they impose a constraint on the behaviour of both Sony and Microsoft . There is abundant evidence that Sony sees both as a competitive threat." All of this and more seems to fold into the conclusion: the PlayStation Store's 30% sales cut is not uncommon (just ask Steam), its pricing wasn't found to be unfair, consumers have many alternatives to Sony's store (currently including physical), and other platforms indirectly enforce price parity by offering user choice. With Sony facing similar cases elsewhere , it'll be interesting to see how lawsuits like this evolve assuming PlayStation ends discs as planned. Eyes will also be glued to PlayStation Store pricing and policy up to and especially after January 2028. PlayStation is "hearing the feedback from customers" on discs, says JRPG boss whose business is built on physical games. sources.title: GTA 6's Game Awards Nominations Are Exactly What Everyone Predicted
sources.text: Going into Tuesday’s reveal of the 2026 Game Awards nominees , the question wasn’t whether or not Grand Theft Auto 6 would pick up any nominations. It was more about how many nominations it would get. And now that the dust has cleared, GTA 6 ’s Game Awards nominations rolled out pretty much…exactly as expected. But it’s nevertheless an unconventional situation. The game isn’t out yet. Reviews haven’t been published. Still, GTA 6 ultimately picked up eight nominations — the most of any game in 2026 , immediately cementing it as a frontrunner for the GOTY race. It was nominated in the following categories: This falls short of records set by Sandfall Interactive’s beloved parry simulator Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , which Polygon’s Oli Welsh predicted was an impossible gambit for GTA 6 anyway. In 2025, Clair Obscur was nominated for 13 categories and won nine awards . That means GTA 6 could win every category it’s nominated in and still fall short of Clair Obscur ’s record. At best, it could tie, depending on how the Player’s Voice category — which is voted on entirely by the public — plays out. As far as sheer number of nominations, purely on grounds of eligibility, it was never going to set the bar. Clair Obscur was up for two categories GTA 6 would never be eligible for (Best Indie Game and Best Debut Indie Game), and its ensemble cast carried it to three Best Performance nominations (Ben Starr, Charlie Cox, and Jennifer English, the latter of whom won). Whatever happens, GTA 6 ’s raft of nominations reveals details about a wildly anticipated game that, to date, has only been seen through selected marketing materials and curated media coverage. A Best Score and Music nomination suggests Grand Theft Auto’s pedigree of killer soundtracks remains unshaken. A Best Game Direction nomination reaffirms Rockstar’s pedigree of immaculately conceived game design. Snagging a Best Narrative nomination — in a year full of narratively rich games that nevertheless excluded the sprawling, ambitious, deliciously messy Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave from the field — suggests GTA 6 might be something more nuanced than a mayhem-packed sandbox. But perhaps the biggest reveal is in Perez’s nomination for Best Performance. The Game Awards did not officially say what role she plays in GTA 6 , but these things tend to go to lead characters, which aligns with a long-standing rumor among fans that Perez portrays Lucia, one of the game’s protagonists. That GTA 6 only nabbed one Best Performance nomination additionally suggests one of two things: that she’s the only good performance in GTA 6 , or that her performance is miles above and beyond everyone else in the game (which includes recent Emmy winner Stephen Root among its officially revealed cast ). A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later. All told, GTA 6 ended up nominated in basically every category it conceivably could’ve been nominated in: the top category, the top of one genre category (games are only allowed to compete in one of those), all three technical categories, and all three general artistic categories. At the top of 2026, much ado was made about the shadow cast by GTA 6 over this year’s GOTY race — if the game was released in time, of course. For a large part of the year, particularly when it was still hard to believe that this thing was actually coming out, when it still felt like it might’ve been delayed, there were hints that this year would fold out in interesting, unexpected ways. On a podium left empty, who clambers to the top? A licensed Star Wars game? A 120-hour tactical soap opera? Another indie darling? None of those ended up nominated for the evening’s top prize. Now that we’re fast approaching the finish line, the race is playing out precisely as many expected a year ago.

sources.text: IGN has conducted a poll on if our readers would be taking time off to play GTA 6 , and nearly half of them said yes. We are officially less than a week away from the release of GTA 6, which means fans are preparing their launch plans as we speak. Economists have estimated that the U.S. economy will incur a $1 billion loss in productivity when the game launches on Thursday due to people calling out sick. We asked IGN readers if they will be part of that drop in productivity , and it seems like a significant amount of them will be. The poll had three options, two of which allowed fans to choose whether or not they'd be using PTO or calling in sick on the day of release. The third choice were for users who plan to go into work on November 19. At the time of writing, over 39,000 users have voted, and 46.5% of them stated that they would be taking the day off to play GTA 6 using either PTO or by calling in sick at launch, while 53.3% stated that they wouldn't be taking time off. The full break down for each poll option is as follows: GTA 6 is expected to have one of the largest entertainment launches of all time and will likely shatter GTA 5's records. Rockstar set new records in 2013 for having the fastest entertainment product to hit $1 billion, with $815 million of that coming in the first day. Given GTA 6 will actually cost more than GTA 5 ($80 for the standard version, $100 for the ultimate edition), it wouldn't be surprising if Rockstar blows way past that. The game has also managed to earn some early praise, as GTA 6 is nominated for eight awards at The Game Awards , including the highly sought-after Game of the Year trophy. To make sure fans are aware of the cultural juggernaut's looming release, Rockstar has been turning Miami into Vice City in real life . The city is currently plastered with in-universe ads for GTA brands, with GTA-branded cars driving all over the place , a Vice City blimp flying over it, and the Miami Heat's arena has even been decked out with Vice City signage. Rockstar also paid $975,000 to install a neon pink sign that reads "Welcome to Vice City." Tomorrow, Rockstar will sponsor a regular season Miami Heat game and turn the team into the Vice City Heat with new jerseys and a never-before-seen court. The game is less than 24 hours from beginning its regional roll out, starting with New Zealand . With all of that said, if you're one of the people skipping work or school play, make sure you pre-load the game so you don't waste a second of your precious time off downloading the game. And while you wait, be sure to check out our interviews with various content creators to see how they're preparing for this gargantuan launch , as well as community members who are preparing to say goodbye to GTA 5 .
